name: Nazca culture
info: The Nazca culture flourished on the desert coast of southern Peru from about 100 BCE to 800 CE, painting polychrome pottery, weaving fine textiles and making the Nazca Lines and the underground aqueducts called puquios.

facts.homeland: The arid southern coast of Peru: the river valleys of the Río Grande de Nazca drainage and the Ica Valley, in today’s Ica Region; key sites the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi and the puquios of Cantalloc
facts.period: Proto Nazca c. 100 BCE–1 CE; Early Nazca c. 1–450 CE; Middle Nazca c. 450–550 CE; Late Nazca c. 550–750 CE; in decline from c. 500 CE and fallen by c. 750 CE
facts.known: the Nazca Lines; puquios, underground aqueducts still in use; polychrome pottery in at least twelve colours; textiles; the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi; trophy heads; trephination and shaped skulls
facts.sources: excavations at Cahuachi and other sites; burials preserved by the dry desert; the nine-phase pottery sequence; ceramic and textile iconography; chemical study of clays; AMS dating of rock varnish in the puquios

t: The Nazca lived in the river valleys of Peru’s southern desert from about 100 BCE to 800 CE, farming with water drawn from underground channels, several dozen of which still work.
Their ceremonial centre at Cahuachi drew whole villages to feasts, where people received the fine painted pottery that carried Nazca images of gods and mythical beings.
They made the Nazca Lines, vast figures and lines on the desert floor whose purpose is still debated, and declined after about 500 CE amid floods and erosion.
dyk: Some Nazca burials have a “head jar” in place of the missing head: a pot painted with a human face, sometimes with plants sprouting from it.
ev: Nazca culture emerges from the Paracas culture on the southern coast of Peru
In the Early Nazca period, the mounds and plazas of Cahuachi are the centre of ritual and feasting
Around the end of Nazca phase 3 or start of phase 4 Cahuachi is abandoned, probably after a drought across the Andes
In the Middle Nazca period the puquios, underground aqueducts, are built
Power shifts from the coast to the highlands with the rise of the Wari culture
Nazca culture has fallen, probably after El Niño floods on a landscape stripped of trees

sections.origins:
The Nazca culture, also spelled Nasca, is the archaeologists’ name for the people who lived in the river valleys of the Río Grande de Nazca drainage and the Ica Valley on the dry southern coast of Peru from about 100 BCE to 800 CE. The Nazca Province of the Ica Region is named after them. They grew out of the Paracas culture of the same coast, known for its complex textiles, and many Nazca traditions came from it.

The shift from Paracas to Nazca is marked in pottery. Paracas potters painted their vessels with resin after firing; Nazca potters began to paint with coloured slips before firing, and this change marks the start of Nazca-style pottery. The culture is generally divided into Proto Nazca (phase 1, c. 100 BCE–1 CE), Early Nazca (phases 2–4, c. 1–450 CE), Middle Nazca (phase 5, c. 450–550 CE) and Late Nazca (phases 6–7, c. 550–750 CE). It belongs to the Early Intermediate Period of Andean archaeology.

Much of what is known comes from the excavations at Cahuachi, the most important site for the study of Nazca culture, and from burials, whose textiles have been preserved by the dry desert. The pottery sequence, divided into nine phases by its changing style, is the main tool for dating Nazca sites, and phases 8 and 9 are now placed in the following Middle Horizon.
sections.society:
Early Nazca society was made up of local chiefdoms and regional centres of power that grew up around Cahuachi, a non-urban ceremonial site of earthwork mounds and plazas in the lower Nazca Valley, first occupied in the late Paracas phase. Its builders shaped natural hills into pyramid mounds. About 70% of the pottery found there is fine polychrome ware and only 30% plain, which led archaeologists to conclude that Cahuachi was a ceremonial centre rather than a town. At festivals people from the surrounding villages came to the centre to feast; ordinary people received valued goods such as painted pottery, while the elite strengthened their power and drew commoners into building work. Cahuachi was abandoned at the end of Nazca phase 3 or the start of phase 4, most scholars believe because of a drought across the Andes, and later Nazca society built fewer large complexes.

The Nazca lived mainly by farming. They ate maize, squash, beans, sweet potato, manioc, achira and peanuts, with some fish, and grew cotton, coca, the San Pedro cactus and gourds. Llamas carried loads and gave wool and meat, and llamas and guinea pigs were sacrificed at Cahuachi.

In the Middle Nazca period they built puquios to farm the desert: underground channels dug into hillsides until they reached the water table, lined with river stones laid without mortar so that water could seep in. The water flowed to irrigation canals or into small reservoirs, and access holes called ojos let people climb down to clear and repair the channels.
sections.beliefs:
Nazca religion, probably shaped by the harsh desert, centred on farming and fertility. Their art shows powerful nature spirits as mythical beings that mix human, animal, bird and fish features: the killer whale, the harvesters, the spotted cat, a serpentine creature and, most often, the Anthropomorphic Mythical Being. Ceremonies took place at Cahuachi, where people worshipped these beings to help their crops grow.

Shamans seem to have played a large part. Pottery and textiles show masked figures, read as ritual specialists in altered states. Shamans apparently used the San Pedro cactus and snuffed the ground seeds of Anadenanthera, and such scenes appear on painted pots, though how to read them is debated and direct archaeological evidence of these plants is very limited.

Severed human heads, called trophy heads, were used in rituals and appear often in Nazca art. Each had a hole in the forehead for a cord, and over a hundred were mummified, a practice found only among the Nazca and the Paracas before them. Early images link them with plants and growth in the “Sprouting Head” motif, and burials suggest the heads may have been of Nazca people rather than outsiders. Their number grew in the Middle Nazca period, perhaps under the pressure of drought, and Late Nazca images suggest that taking heads added to a leader’s prestige. Many burials are partial, and some replace the missing head with a painted head jar.
sections.arts:
Nazca pottery is painted in at least twelve colours, in shapes such as double-spout bottles, bowls, cups, vases and effigies. Phase 1 shows fruits, plants, people and animals realistically; phases 2–4 set their subjects against bold red, black or white grounds; phase 5 adds rays and scrolls to supernatural figures; and in phases 6 and 7 the mythical figures sprout so many rays and tassels that the style is called “proliferous”, with more warlike scenes and some influence from the Moche culture of the north coast. Like other early South American societies, the Nazca had no writing; the images on their pottery carried meaning instead.

Nazca textiles, woven probably by women on backstrap looms from cotton and wool, carried the same motifs, often before they appeared on pots. Almost every body was buried wrapped in cloth, with shawls, dresses, tunics, belts and bags among the grave goods. Mary Frame’s study of textiles from Cahuachi showed that women had access to high-status materials and wore sacred imagery.

The Nazca Lines are geometric shapes, long lines and huge animal figures, some as large as a football field, made by large organised work groups who removed the red surface pebbles to expose the lighter ground. Some think they were made for the gods to see, others that they were a calendar for planting and harvest, or paths for processions; no theory has been proved. The Nazca also practised trephination, removing pieces of skull from living people, some of whom survived, and shaped infants’ heads by binding.
sections.exchange:
The Nazca world was linked by its ceremonial centre. Clays matching the chemical signature of polychrome pottery found across the southern Nazca region come from near Cahuachi, although there is no clear evidence that pottery was made there. The site was most likely a centre where fine pottery was handed out, and pilgrims and feasters carried it home, spreading the culture of the ruling class. Polychrome pottery has been found among all classes of Nazca society. Spondylus shells and traces of gold were also found at Cahuachi.

The Nazca shared the coast with other cultures. They inherited much from the Paracas, and Nazca art of phases 6 and 7 shows influence from the Moche of northern Peru. Warlike motifs grew more common from phase 5, which some link to conflict caused by drought. In the last phases power shifted from the coast to the highlands, with the rise of the Wari culture around 650 CE, and the disjointed figures and geometric designs of Nazca phase 8 belong to this new age.
sections.legacy:
From about 500 CE Nazca society declined, and by about 750 CE it had fallen. A likely cause is an El Niño that brought widespread, destructive floods. The Nazca may have made these worse by gradually cutting down Prosopis pallida trees to clear land for maize and cotton. These trees held the landscape together against river and wind erosion, and without them the land was exposed to sudden changes of climate, eroding the soil and leaving irrigation channels high and dry.

Much of their work survives. The dry desert has preserved the Nazca Lines for centuries, and Nazca and Paracas textiles make up most of what is known about early weaving in the region. Several dozen puquios still carry water today, some altered with motor pumps and concrete-lined reservoirs, and some of the best preserved are at Cantalloc.

The Nazca Lines have been studied by anthropologists, archaeologists and astronomers, who have not found conclusive evidence for any of the theories about their purpose. The term “trophy head”, coined by the archaeologist Max Uhle, comes from his reading of severed heads in ancient Peruvian art as trophies of war, though early Nazca pottery suggests that their first purpose may have been tied to farming.

summary: The Nazca culture flourished on the desert coast of southern Peru from about 100 BCE to 800 CE, growing out of the Paracas culture. Its people farmed with water from underground puquios, gathered for feasts at the ceremonial centre of Cahuachi, and made polychrome pottery, fine textiles and the Nazca Lines. Weakened by floods and erosion, the culture declined from about 500 CE as power passed to the highland Wari.

notes: Dates kept: -100 to 800, as in the article's lede. The article's own phases end at 750 CE and it says the culture 'had fallen completely' by 750; 800 is kept as the lede's end.

The article contradicts itself on trophy heads in the Late Nazca period (one sentence: their number 'reaches its peak'; another: it 'tapered off'). I wrote only that Middle Nazca numbers grew and that Late Nazca imagery links head-taking with leaders' prestige.

The dating of Cahuachi's abandonment as 'c. 450 CE' in the events is my placement of 'the very end of Nazca 3/early Nazca 4' on the article's phase table (Early Nazca = phases 2–4, 1–450 CE); the editor may prefer the phase wording alone.
The 'Paracas Textile' in the Brooklyn Museum (300 BCE–100 CE) is discussed in the article's Nazca textiles section but is named Paracas; left out to avoid misattribution.
